confusionCorner.body: The chi‑square method for variance confidence intervals requires that the population be [[imp:normally distributed]]. If the data are heavily skewed, the confidence interval may not be accurate. Always check for approximate normality before applying this method.
confusionCorner.title: Normality Is Critical

explanation: The [[kw:chi‑square distribution]] ($\chi^2$) is used to construct confidence intervals for a population variance $\sigma^2$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ when the population is [[imp:normally distributed]].
The point estimate for $\sigma^2$ is the sample variance $s^2$, and for $\sigma$ it is the sample standard deviation $s$.
The chi‑square distribution is a family of curves, each determined by its [[kw:degrees of freedom]]: $d.f. = n - 1$.

Key properties: (1) All chi‑square values are $\ge 0$. (2) The distribution is [[imp:positively skewed]] (right‑skewed), especially for small d.f. (3) As d.f. increases, the distribution becomes more symmetric and approaches a normal shape. (4) The total area under any chi‑square curve is 1.

rows.1: Positively skewed (right‑skewed); becomes more symmetric as d.f. increases

discoveryHook.scenario: In manufacturing, variation can be just as important as the average. If the lengths of bolts vary too much, some won't fit. The chi‑square distribution allows us to build confidence intervals for variance and standard deviation—giving us a way to measure and control consistency.

examples.prompt: A random sample of 20 bolts has a sample standard deviation of 0.5 inch. If we want to build a confidence interval for the population variance, how many degrees of freedom will the chi‑square distribution have?
examples.title: Example A – Degrees of Freedom
steps: Degrees of freedom for variance estimation: $d.f. = n - 1$.
We will use the chi‑square distribution with 19 degrees of freedom.
With small $n$, the sample variance $s^2$ varies a lot, so the distribution of $(n-1)s^2/\sigma^2$ is spread out and skewed.
As $n$ increases, the sample variance becomes a more reliable estimator, and the chi‑square distribution approaches a normal shape.
In fact, for large d.f., the chi‑square distribution is approximately normal with mean $d.f.$ and variance $2(d.f.)$.

confusionCorner.title: Which Area for Which Critical Value?
confusionCorner.body: The area to the right of $\chi^2_R$ is the small tail area $(1-c)/2$; the area to the right of $\chi^2_L$ is the large area $(1+c)/2$. [[imp:Always double‑check that $\chi^2_R > \chi^2_L$; if they're reversed, you've swapped the areas.]]

formulaCard.title: Google Sheets for Chi‑Square Critical Values

explanation: For a given confidence level $c$, there are two critical values: $\chi^2_R$ (right‑tail critical value) and $\chi^2_L$ (left‑tail critical value).
The area to the right of $\chi^2_R$ is $\frac{1-c}{2}$, and the area to the right of $\chi^2_L$ is $\frac{1+c}{2}$.
These values are found in the chi‑square distribution table (Table 6) using $d.f. = n-1$ and the appropriate right‑tail areas.

In Google Sheets: use `=CHISQ.INV.RT(probability, deg_freedom)` to find the value with a given right‑tail area. For $\chi^2_R$: `=CHISQ.INV.RT((1-c)/2, d.f.)`. For $\chi^2_L$: `=CHISQ.INV.RT((1+c)/2, d.f.)`.

steps: For $\sigma$: $\sqrt{0.80} \approx 0.89$ and $\sqrt{3.18} \approx 1.78$. So $0.89 < \sigma < 1.78$ mg.
We are 99% confident the population variance is between 0.80 and 3.18, and the standard deviation is between 0.89 and 1.78 mg.
Dividing by a larger number makes the fraction smaller.
Since $\chi^2_R > \chi^2_L$, the term $(n-1)s^2/\chi^2_R$ gives the lower (smaller) bound.
The term $(n-1)s^2/\chi^2_L$ gives the upper (larger) bound.
This correctly places the confidence interval with the larger spread on the right, reflecting the chi‑square skewness.

confusionCorner.body: A common mistake is to put $\chi^2_L$ in the denominator of the lower bound and $\chi^2_R$ in the upper bound. That would reverse the interval. [[imp:Remember: larger critical value → smaller fraction → lower bound; smaller critical value → larger fraction → upper bound.]]

The formula places the larger critical value in the denominator of the lower bound and the smaller critical value in the denominator of the upper bound—making the interval wider on the right, reflecting the skewness of the chi‑square distribution.

visuals.title: 99% Confidence Intervals for Allergy Medicine Weights ($n=30$, $s=1.20$)

explanation: A [[kw:c-confidence interval for the population variance $\sigma^2$]] is: $$\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_R} < \sigma^2 < \frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_L}$$

The confidence interval for the population standard deviation $\sigma$ is obtained by taking the square root of each endpoint: $$\sqrt{\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_R}} < \sigma < \sqrt{\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\chi^2_L}}$$

Note that the [[imp:larger]] critical value $\chi^2_R$ appears in the denominator of the lower bound, and the [[imp:smaller]] critical value $\chi^2_L$ appears in the denominator of the upper bound. This is because variance is inversely related to the chi‑square statistic.
The interval is not symmetric around $s^2$ because the chi‑square distribution is skewed.

explanation: Confidence intervals for $\sigma$ are used to assess whether the variability of a process meets specifications.
If the entire confidence interval for $\sigma$ lies below a specified maximum allowable standard deviation, we can be confident the process is consistent enough.
If the upper bound of the interval exceeds the limit, the process may need adjustment.
As with other confidence intervals, the interpretation is: 'We are $c$% confident that the true population standard deviation lies between the lower and upper bounds.'

discoveryHook.scenario: Chi‑square confidence intervals follow a distinct blueprint because of the two different critical values and their placement. By systematically working through Understand‑Solve‑Conclude, you can avoid the common mistake of swapping the critical values.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid: Solving Chi‑Square Confidence Interval Problems

legend.meaning: $\chi^2_R$ (larger) in lower bound denominator; $\chi^2_L$ (smaller) in upper bound denominator.

explanation: Blueprint steps: [[imp:Understand → Solve → Conclude]].
1. [[kw:Understand]]: Verify the population is normally distributed. Identify $n$, $s$ (or $s^2$), and confidence level $c$. Determine $d.f. = n-1$.

2. [[kw:Solve]]: Find the right‑tail areas: $(1-c)/2$ and $(1+c)/2$. Use the chi‑square table or `=CHISQ.INV.RT` to get $\chi^2_R$ and $\chi^2_L$. Compute the lower bound: $(n-1)s^2 / \chi^2_R$, and upper bound: $(n-1)s^2 / \chi^2_L$. For $\sigma$, take square roots.

3. [[kw:Conclude]]: State the confidence interval for $\sigma^2$ and/or $\sigma$. Interpret: 'We are $c$% confident that the true population variance is between … and …'. Check if the interval meets any specification limits.

rows.1: We are 98% confident that the true standard deviation of waiting times is between 2.64 and 5.53 minutes.

confusionCorner.body: If you accidentally swap the critical values, the lower bound will be larger than the upper bound. [[imp:Always verify that $\chi^2_R$ is the larger value and $\chi^2_L$ is the smaller.]]
confusionCorner.title: Double‑Check $\chi^2_R > \chi^2_L$

steps: Solve: Right‑tail areas 0.005 and 0.995. $\chi^2_R = 35.718$, $\chi^2_L = 5.697$ (from table or Sheets).
Lower bound for $\sigma^2$: $(17 \times 0.0841)/35.718 \approx 0.0400$. Upper: $(17 \times 0.0841)/5.697 \approx 0.251$.
Lower bound for $\sigma$: $\sqrt{0.0400} \approx 0.20$ hr. Upper: $\sqrt{0.251} \approx 0.50$ hr.
Conclude: We are 99% confident the true standard deviation of reserve capacities is between 0.20 and 0.50 hour.

title: Confidence Intervals for Variance and Standard Deviation
presenterNotes: Block 1: Emphasize the shape of the chi‑square distribution and the normality assumption. Use visual comparisons of different d.f.
Block 2: Practice finding critical values from the table. The Google Sheets functions CHISQ.INV.RT make this easier. Highlight that we need two values.
Block 3: Walk through the construction carefully. The placement of $\chi^2_R$ and $\chi^2_L$ is crucial. Use the allergy medicine example to show the full process.
Block 4: Connect to quality control. Interpreting whether a specification is met gives real‑world motivation.
Block 5: The blueprint provides a structured approach. Emphasize checking normality and verifying that $\chi^2_R > \chi^2_L$.
